questions.stem: Why did Icarus fall into the sea and drown?
questions.successCriteria: Student can identify the correct cause of Icarus's fall.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Question directly tests reading comprehension of plot events.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of the plot cause-effect: Icarus flew too high.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks Icarus flew too low or that the wings broke for another reason.

options.label: A
options.text: He flew too low and the seawater weighed down his wings.
options.feedbackWrong: Actually, Daedalus warned Icarus not to fly too low, but the fall was because he flew too high.

options.label: B
options.text: He flew too high and the sun melted the wax on his wings.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Icarus ignored his father's warning, flew too close to the sun, and the wax melted.

options.label: C
options.text: His wings were poorly made and broke apart.
options.feedbackWrong: Daedalus made strong wings. They broke only because the wax melted from the sun's heat.

options.label: D
options.text: He was pushed by a gust of wind.
options.feedbackWrong: No, the story says he fell because the wax melted, not because of wind.

questions.successCriteria: Student can distinguish between the reason for banishment and imprisonment.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Question tests understanding of cause and effect in the myth.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of the sequence: banishment was due to jealousy and attempted murder.
questions.commonMisconception: Student confuses banishment (Athens) with imprisonment in Crete.

options.label: A
options.text: He built the Labyrinth for King Minos.
options.feedbackWrong: Building the Labyrinth happened in Crete, after his banishment.

options.label: B
options.text: He tried to kill his nephew Perdix out of jealousy.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Daedalus was jealous of Perdix's talent and pushed him off a cliff, so he was banished.

options.label: C
options.text: He helped Queen Pasiphae hide the Minotaur.
options.feedbackWrong: That happened later in Crete, not the reason for his banishment from Athens.

options.label: D
options.text: He stole a precious artifact from the Athenian temple.
options.feedbackWrong: No, the myth does not mention this. His crime was against Perdix.

questions.stem: Can the myth of Daedalus and Icarus have more than one valid theme? Explain using evidence from the story.

questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.

questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands that myths can have multiple themes and can support with evidence.

questions.sampleStrongAnswer: Yes, the myth can have multiple themes. For example, one theme is 'heed warnings.' Icarus ignored Daedalus's warning not to fly too high, and he fell. Another theme is 'avoid overconfidence.' Icarus thought he could fly higher and failed.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect cause for Icarus's fall (e.g., flying too low).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes Icarus fell because he flew too low and the seawater weighed down his wings. However, in the myth, Icarus flew too high, causing the sun to melt the wax on his wings, leading to his fall.

miniLesson.explain: Icarus fell because he ignored his father's warning and flew too high. The heat from the sun melted the wax holding his wings together. He did not fly too low; in fact, Daedalus warned him not to fly too low either, but the fatal mistake was flying too high.
miniLesson.example: In the story, Daedalus builds wings from feathers and wax. He tells Icarus to fly at a medium height. Icarus becomes overconfident and flies higher. The wax melts, his wings fall apart, and he plummets into the sea.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Too high, sun melts wax. Too low, sea dampens wings. Icarus chose too high.

guidedPractice.prompt: Did Icarus fly too high or too low?
Why did the wax on Icarus's wings melt?
guidedPractice.answer: Because he flew too close to the sun.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain what would have happened if Icarus had listened to his father's warning about flying too high.
guidedPractice.answer: His wings would have stayed intact, and he would have survived the flight.

reteachModules.trigger: Student thinks Daedalus was banished for building the Labyrinth or for helping Pasiphae.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Confusing the reason for Daedalus's banishment from Athens (jealousy and attempted murder of Perdix) with the reason for his imprisonment in Crete (hiding Pasiphae's secret).

miniLesson.explain: Daedalus was banished from Athens because he tried to kill his nephew Perdix out of jealousy. Later, in Crete, he was imprisoned by King Minos for helping Queen Pasiphae hide the Minotaur's secret. These are two separate events: banishment from Athens, imprisonment in Crete.
miniLesson.example: Think of it like being expelled from one school for fighting (banishment) and then being grounded at a new school for breaking a rule (imprisonment). The reasons are different.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Jealousy = banishment from Athens; Secrets = imprisonment in Crete.

guidedPractice.prompt: What caused Daedalus to be banished from Athens? (A) Building the Labyrinth (B) Trying to kill his nephew Perdix (C) Helping Queen Pasiphae
Explain why Daedalus was banished from Athens but then later imprisoned in Crete. How are these two events different?
guidedPractice.answer: Daedalus was banished for attempting to murder his nephew Perdix out of jealousy. Later, he was imprisoned in Crete because he helped Queen Pasiphae hide the secret of the Minotaur. The banishment was punishment for a crime in Athens; the imprisonment was because King Minos wanted to keep him from revealing the secret.

guidedPractice.prompt: Create a short story or analogy that clearly distinguishes between Daedalus's banishment and his imprisonment. Use the key vocabulary: jealous, attempt murder, banished, imprisoned, secret.
guidedPractice.answer: Daedalus was a talented inventor, but his jealousy of his nephew made him commit a terrible act. He pushed Perdix off a cliff, so he was banished from Athens. In Crete, he built the Labyrinth and kept the Minotaur's secret. When the king learned of his help, he was imprisoned. So, jealousy led to banishment; keeping a secret led to imprisonment.

reteachModules.trigger: Student chooses incorrect answer in diagnostic question about character roles, e.g., selecting King Minos as Icarus's father or Icarus as inventor.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student confuses the roles of characters in the Daedalus and Icarus myth, such as thinking Daedalus is a king or Icarus is the inventor.

miniLesson.explain: In the myth of Daedalus and Icarus, each character has a specific role. Daedalus is an inventor and craftsman, not a king. He is the father of Icarus and uncle of Perdix. Icarus is Daedalus's son, not an inventor. King Minos is the ruler of Crete, not a craftsman. Understanding these roles helps you follow the story.
miniLesson.example: Daedalus built the Labyrinth for King Minos. He also made wings for himself and Icarus to escape. Icarus flew too close to the sun and fell. King Minos did not build anything; he gave orders.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Daedalus designs, Icarus flies, Minos rules.

guidedPractice.prompt: Who is the inventor in the myth of Daedalus and Icarus?
Is Icarus the inventor or the son of Daedalus?
Explain why King Minos is not the one who built the Labyrinth.
guidedPractice.answer: King Minos is the ruler who ordered the Labyrinth to be built, but Daedalus, the inventor and craftsman, actually constructed it.

reteachModules.trigger: Student stated that a myth can only have one valid theme.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes a myth can only have one correct theme, but the teacher explained that multiple valid themes can be supported by text evidence.

miniLesson.explain: A theme is a central message or lesson in a story. Myths often contain multiple themes because they can be interpreted in different ways. For example, the myth of Daedalus and Icarus teaches about heeding warnings, avoiding overconfidence, and respecting experience. All of these are valid as long as you can support them with evidence from the text.
miniLesson.example: One student might say the theme is 'listen to your elders' because Daedalus warned Icarus. Another student might say the theme is 'pride comes before a fall' because Icarus's overconfidence led to his death. Both are correct if they use evidence.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a multi-tool: one story has many lessons. Like a Swiss Army knife has different tools, a myth can have multiple themes.

guidedPractice.prompt: Is it true or false? A myth can only have one theme.
guidedPractice.answer: False. A myth can have multiple themes.

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at the story of Daedalus and Icarus. One theme is 'heed warnings.' Can you think of another valid theme? Use evidence from the story.
guidedPractice.answer: Another theme is 'avoid overconfidence.' Evidence: Icarus flew too high despite his father's warning, and his wax wings melted.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain in your own words why it is important to recognize that a myth can have multiple themes. Give an example from the myth or from real life.
guidedPractice.answer: It is important because it shows that stories can teach different lessons to different people. For example, the myth of Daedalus and Icarus can teach about the dangers of overconfidence, but also about the importance of following advice. In real life, a news story about a business failure might have themes of greed, poor planning, or lack of teamwork.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected a definition that describes a simple maze with exits.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: A labyrinth is the same as a simple maze that you can find your way out of.

miniLesson.explain: A labyrinth is different from a simple maze. In Greek mythology, the Labyrinth built by Daedalus had only one entrance and no exit. It was a confusing, winding structure designed to trap the Minotaur forever. People could easily get lost inside and never find their way out. Modern mazes often have multiple paths and exits, but the original Labyrinth was a single path that twisted and turned, leading to the center with no escape.
miniLesson.example: Think of the Labyrinth in the story: King Minos used it to imprison the Minotaur. No one who entered could escape except Theseus, who used a ball of thread to retrace his steps. This shows its unique design.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Labyrinth = 'Lost and never leave' (one entrance, no exit). Maze = 'Maybe escape' (multiple exits). The Labyrinth is like a trap, not a puzzle you solve.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the main difference between a labyrinth and a simple maze?
guidedPractice.answer: A labyrinth has one entrance and no exit, while a simple maze can have multiple exits and paths.

guidedPractice.prompt: In the myth, why did Daedalus design the Labyrinth with no exit instead of making it possible to escape?
guidedPractice.answer: King Minos wanted to imprison the Minotaur forever, so Daedalus built the Labyrinth with no exit to ensure the monster could never leave.

guidedPractice.prompt: Imagine you are explaining the word 'labyrinth' to a classmate. Write a short paragraph that contrasts the Labyrinth in the myth with a typical maze you might find in a cornfield.
guidedPractice.answer: The Labyrinth in the Greek myth is different from a typical corn maze because it was designed as a prison with only one entrance and no way out. While a corn maze often has multiple paths and exits for enjoyment, the Labyrinth was a deadly trap. So, a labyrinth is not just any maze; it's a specific kind of maze with no exit.

questions.stem: In the myth of Daedalus and Icarus, the class discussed several possible themes. Which of the following statements about themes is correct?
options: A myth can only have one theme that everyone agrees on.
A myth can have multiple valid themes as long as each is supported by evidence.
A myth's theme must be explicitly stated in the text.
Themes in myths are always about pride.

questions.stem: Apart from the theme of 'heeding warnings,' identify another possible theme from the myth of Daedalus and Icarus. Use specific evidence from the story to support your theme.
questions.rubric: Student identifies a different valid theme (e.g., overconfidence leads to downfall, respecting experience, balance). Provides at least one piece of text evidence (e.g., Icarus flew too high despite warning; Daedalus's advice). Must be a theme, not a plot summary.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the Labyrinth built by Daedalus in the myth?
options: A winding structure with one entrance and no exit
A simple maze with multiple exits
A straight path to the center
A building with many rooms and doors

questions.stem: In your own words, explain the difference between a labyrinth and a simple maze, using the story of Daedalus and Icarus as an example.
questions.rubric: Student must state that a labyrinth has no exit (or is a trap), while a simple maze has exits. Reference to Daedalus's Labyrinth imprisoning the Minotaur is expected.

retestCards.passRule: Select the correct definition and provide an explanation that clearly distinguishes labyrinth from maze, referencing the myth.

cards.question: Why did Icarus fall into the sea and drown?
options: He flew too low and the seawater weighed down his wings.
He flew too high and the sun melted the wax on his wings.
His wings were poorly made and broke apart.
He was pushed by a gust of wind.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of the plot cause-effect: Icarus flew too high.
misconceptions: Actually, Daedalus warned Icarus not to fly too low, but the fall was because he flew too high.
✓ Correct! Icarus ignored his father's warning, flew too close to the sun, and the wax melted.
Daedalus made strong wings. They broke only because the wax melted from the sun's heat.
No, the story says he fell because the wax melted, not because of wind.
cards.successCriteria: Student can identify the correct cause of Icarus's fall.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Question directly tests reading comprehension of plot events.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks Icarus flew too low or that the wings broke for another reason.

cards.question: Why was Daedalus banished from Athens?
options: He built the Labyrinth for King Minos.
He tried to kill his nephew Perdix out of jealousy.
He helped Queen Pasiphae hide the Minotaur.
He stole a precious artifact from the Athenian temple.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of the sequence: banishment was due to jealousy and attempted murder.
misconceptions: Building the Labyrinth happened in Crete, after his banishment.
✓ Correct! Daedalus was jealous of Perdix's talent and pushed him off a cliff, so he was banished.
That happened later in Crete, not the reason for his banishment from Athens.
No, the myth does not mention this. His crime was against Perdix.
cards.successCriteria: Student can distinguish between the reason for banishment and imprisonment.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Question tests understanding of cause and effect in the myth.
cards.commonMisconception: Student confuses banishment (Athens) with imprisonment in Crete.

cards.question: Look at the character relationship diagram below. Who is Icarus's father?
options: Daedalus
King Minos
Perdix
Pasiphae
cards.diagnosis: Check that student can read a simple character relationship diagram and identify family roles.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! The diagram shows Daedalus as the father of Icarus.
King Minos is the ruler of Crete, not Icarus's father.
Perdix was Daedalus's nephew; he is not related to Icarus in that way.
Pasiphae was the queen of Crete; she is not Icarus's father.
cards.successCriteria: Student can identify Daedalus as Icarus's father from the diagram.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Question tests character identification through a visual diagram.
cards.commonMisconception: Student may confuse Daedalus with other male characters or think the diagram shows something else.

cards.question: Can the myth of Daedalus and Icarus have more than one valid theme? Explain using evidence from the story.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that myths can have multiple themes and can support with evidence.
cards.successCriteria: Student acknowledges multiple themes possible and provides at least one theme with evidence.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Question evaluates theme analysis and recognition of multiple valid interpretations.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks only one correct theme exists.
